name: El Silbón
description: A cursed wandering spirit of the Venezuelan and Colombian Llanos who carries his murdered father's bones in a sack and whose whistle reverses with distance: close-sounding when far, distant-sounding when very near.
full_description: El Silbón ('the whistler') is a legendary spirit of the Llanos region of Venezuela — particularly Portuguesa state and Guanarito Municipality — and of Colombia's Eastern Llanos, said to have arisen as a folk legend in the mid-19th century. According to the most widely told version, El Silbón was a spoiled son who, in a drunken rage, killed his father, and (in some versions) prepared the body as food for his unsuspecting mother; on discovering the truth, his grandfather whipped him, rubbed lemon and pepper into his wounds, and cursed him to wander forever, carrying his father's bones in a sack. He appears as the shadow of a tall, gaunt man, sometimes wearing a hat; in some accounts as a six-metre giant moving among the treetops. His characteristic whistle is held to be inverted in distance: when it sounds near, he is far; when it sounds faint and distant, he is dangerously close. He preys particularly on drunkards and unfaithful husbands. Folkloric protections include a barking dog (the only thing he reportedly fears), chili peppers, and a whip — items linked to the curse imposed by his grandfather.
origin: Folkloric range across the Llanos savanna of Venezuela and the Eastern Llanos of Colombia, with the densest tradition in the Venezuelan state of Portuguesa.

etymology.origin: Spanish 'el silbón', literally 'the whistler' or 'the one who whistles', from the verb 'silbar' (to whistle).
etymology.first_use: Recorded in 19th-century Llanero oral tradition; widely standardised in 20th-century Venezuelan folkloric literature.

timeline.event: El Silbón legend takes shape in Venezuelan Llanero oral tradition (per Wikipedia)
Rómulo Gallegos publishes 'Cantaclaro', situating the Llanos in modern Venezuelan literary imagination and creating an audience for Llanero folklore
timeline.significance: Cultural context for 20th-century literary engagement with Llanero folklore

cultural_notes: Hearing the whistle is itself an omen; if the whistle sounds close, no immediate danger; if it sounds far, the listener is in immediate peril. Protection is sought through dogs, chili pepper, and the whip.
